Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Rebecca, a forty-year-old data scientist, had always thought of herself as someone who could handle anything with logic and hard work. That belief had been her anchor through years of building a career in a competitive field, through the careful routines of married life in a suburban neighborhood that felt safe precisely because it was predictable. But that anchor had been ripped away on an evening she could not stop reliving, even though she had tried everything to escape it.

It had happened six months ago, on a late autumn afternoon. Rebecca had taken a wrong turn while driving home from a client meeting, her GPS rerouting her through a stretch of road she had never seen before. The road passed the edge of a small Arab village, a place she had only ever glimpsed from the highway. As she slowed at a curve, she saw the flames. A building at the village’s edge was burning, and in the dimming light she could make out figures running, shouting in a language she did not understand. Then she saw a woman collapse near the road, her clothing on fire, and a man trying to beat out the flames with his bare hands. Rebecca had stopped the car, her hands frozen on the wheel. She had not gotten out. She had not called for help for what felt like an eternity. By the time she dialed 911, the woman was no longer moving. The fire trucks arrived too late.

In the weeks that followed, Rebecca tried to bury the memory under the weight of her work. As a data scientist, she was used to losing herself in spreadsheets, algorithms, and the clean logic of numbers. She began arriving at the office before dawn and leaving after midnight, taking on projects her colleagues declined, volunteering for extra reports. Her husband, Mark, started leaving dinner in the refrigerator with notes she would find untouched the next morning. She told herself that staying busy was the only way to keep functioning, that if she stopped moving, something terrible would catch up with her. But the memories did not wait for stillness. They came without warning: the smell of smoke in a neighbor’s barbecue, the flicker of a candle at a restaurant, the sight of a red taillight on the highway. In those moments, she would feel the heat on her face again, hear the screams in her ears, and for a terrifying instant she was back in that car, watching the woman burn. She would come back to herself shaking, her heart pounding, certain for a few seconds that she was still there.

The memories themselves felt wrong, too. When Rebecca tried to recall what she had for breakfast that morning, the image was flat and distant, like a photograph faded with age. But the memory of the fire was sharp, three-dimensional, almost more real than the room she was standing in. She could hear the crackling, the desperate shouts, the sound of her own breath catching in her throat. These intrusions had no respect for time or place. She would be in a meeting, explaining a regression model, and suddenly the sound of a police siren outside would send her back, and she would have to excuse herself to the bathroom, gripping the sink until her hands stopped trembling.

Rebecca began to believe that she had failed in a way that could never be undone. She replayed the moment over and over: she could have gotten out of the car, she could have run to the woman, she could have done something. Somebody else would have acted, she told herself. Somebody braver, somebody less frozen. She was certain that other people would never have gotten into that situation in the first place—they would have known which road to avoid, would have sensed the danger, would have been better prepared. The thought that she had been helpless, that she had watched and done nothing, began to hollow her out. She started checking the locks on her doors and windows three, four times before bed, and again when she woke up. Strangers approaching her in the grocery store parking lot made her chest tighten; she crossed the street to avoid anyone who looked like they might ask for directions or a moment of her time.

At work, her productivity began to falter. She was spending more hours at her desk but accomplishing less, her mind wandering back to that evening, trying to make sense of why it had happened to her. She went over the event again and again in her head, searching for a meaning she could not find, as if understanding it might undo the guilt. But no answer came, and the rumination only left her more exhausted. She stopped answering calls from her mother, declined invitations from friends, and began to feel that none of it mattered anyway. Late at night, alone in her home office while Mark slept, she found herself wondering if her life was worth continuing. The thought frightened her, but it also felt honest.

What finally brought Rebecca to seek help was a morning when she could not get out of bed. She lay staring at the ceiling, the memory of the flames so vivid that she could almost feel the heat on her skin, and she realized she no longer knew what she was working for, or why she was still trying to hold everything together. She called a therapist that afternoon, her voice flat and mechanical as she explained that she needed an appointment. She was afraid of what she might find if she opened the door to all of this, but she was more afraid of what would happen if she did not.
